subtopic_detail: Microcytic anaemia with pica and loss of acquired skills in a toddler
stem:
A 2 year old boy is brought to your clinic with three months of irritability, poor appetite and constipation. His family moved six months ago into a weatherboard cottage built in the 1920s that is being sanded and repainted around them.

His mother says he chews the window sills and eats flakes of paint from the floor. She is most worried that he used to say about twenty words and now says only five. He was born at term and his development was previously normal. He drinks about 400 mL of cow milk a day and eats meat three times a week. Iron studies taken by another doctor two weeks ago showed a ferritin of 38 micrograms per litre.

data_table.Examination: Pale, mildly irritable but consolable, abdomen soft with no organomegaly, no neurological focal signs, gait normal
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (110-140), mean cell volume 68 fL (75-87), ferritin 38 micrograms per litre (20-100), reticulocytes 1.2 percent, blood film shows basophilic stippling
data_table.Social: Home built in the 1920s currently being sanded and repainted

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Send a venous blood lead level today
options.rationale: Microcytic anaemia with basophilic stippling and a ferritin that is not low excludes iron deficiency as the explanation, and the combination of pica, renovation of a pre 1970 house, constipation and loss of acquired language points to lead. A venous sample is used because capillary samples are readily contaminated by lead on the skin. (Source: NHMRC: Lead exposure and health effects in Australia)
source_refs: NHMRC: Lead exposure and health effects in Australia

options.rationale: Thalassaemia trait also gives microcytosis with a preserved ferritin, but it does not cause basophilic stippling with developmental regression, and it would not explain the pica or the constipation. Iron studies have already been done and are not low. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

Coeliac disease is a reasonable cause of microcytic anaemia with poor appetite, but it usually does so by producing iron deficiency, and the ferritin here is preserved. It does not account for basophilic stippling or for loss of language. (Source: RCH CPG: Anaemia)

Hearing assessment is essential in any child losing language and should follow, but it does not explain the anaemia, the stippled film or the pica, and it would miss an ongoing and reversible exposure. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay)

options.text: Start oral iron and recheck in a month
options.rationale: Empirical iron is the usual response to a microcytic anaemia in a toddler, but with a ferritin of 38 micrograms per litre the anaemia is not iron deficient, and a month of treatment leaves the child in the exposed house. Lead also impairs haem synthesis independently of iron status. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

explanation.summary: Lead poisoning in Australian toddlers is now uncommon but persists where pre 1970 lead paint is disturbed by renovation. The clinical signature is insidious: irritability, constipation, poor appetite, pica and, importantly, loss of previously acquired developmental skills. The haematological clue is a microcytic anaemia with basophilic stippling in a child whose ferritin is not low, which uncouples the anaemia from the usual dietary iron deficiency. Diagnosis is by venous blood lead level, and the first management step is always removal from the source of exposure.
key_points: Basophilic stippling with a preserved ferritin separates lead from ordinary iron deficiency
Renovation of housing built before 1970 is the dominant Australian exposure route
Use a venous rather than capillary sample because skin contamination causes false elevation
Developmental regression, not just delay, should always prompt a search for an acquired cause
explanation.pearls: Australian notification and intervention thresholds start at a blood lead of 5 micrograms per decilitre, and chelation is reserved for levels above 45 micrograms per decilitre or for encephalopathy; below that, removing the exposure is the treatment.

sources.label: NHMRC: Lead exposure and health effects in Australia

subtopic_detail: Collapse at ten days of life with absent femoral pulses
stem:
You are the registrar in a regional emergency department when a 10 day old boy is brought in by ambulance. His mother says he fed poorly overnight, then this morning went grey and floppy and felt cold to touch from the tummy down.

He was born at term by normal vaginal birth with no antenatal concerns and was discharged well on day two. Brachial pulses are easily felt but femoral pulses cannot be palpated on either side. There is no murmur. Pre ductal saturation is 96 percent in the right hand and post ductal saturation is 88 percent in the right foot. Blood glucose is 3.8 mmol/L and there is no rash.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 186 beats per minute, blood pressure 62/38 mmHg in the right arm, respiratory rate 68 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent pre ductal and 88 percent post ductal, temperature 36.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mottled and cool peripheries with capillary refill 5 seconds, liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin, brachial pulses present, femoral pulses impalpable bilaterally, no murmur
data_table.Investigations: Venous lactate 7.2 mmol/L (less than 2), pH 7.18, base excess minus 12, blood glucose 3.8 mmol/L, chest radiograph shows cardiomegaly with pulmonary venous congestion
data_table.Birth history: Term vaginal birth, discharged well on day two, newborn examination documented as normal

lead_in: What is the most important immediate treatment?

options.text: Give a 20 mL/kg sodium chloride 0.9 percent bolus
options.rationale: Large volume loading in a neonate whose shock is obstructive rather than hypovolaemic worsens pulmonary oedema, and the enlarged liver and radiographic congestion already indicate a fluid loaded circulation. Small cautious aliquots may be used but volume is not the treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital heart disease in the newborn)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital heart disease in the newborn

options.text: Start an intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion
options.rationale: A collapse in the second week with absent femoral pulses and a saturation step down between the right hand and the foot is duct dependent systemic circulation, and prostaglandin E1 reopens the arterial duct to restore flow to the lower body while transfer is arranged. It is started before echocardiography because the diagnosis is clinical and the duct is closing. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital heart disease in the newborn)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital heart disease in the newborn

options.rationale: Late onset sepsis presents similarly and antibiotics should be given after cultures, but they do nothing about a closing duct, and the pre ductal to post ductal saturation gradient with impalpable femoral pulses is structural rather than infective. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis)

options.text: Give intravenous frusemide for the pulmonary congestion
options.rationale: Diuresis addresses a consequence of the obstruction rather than its cause, and reducing preload in an infant dependent on ductal flow to perfuse the lower body can precipitate further collapse. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital heart disease in the newborn)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital heart disease in the newborn

options.text: Arrange urgent echocardiography before any treatment
options.rationale: Echocardiography defines the lesion and should be arranged, but withholding treatment until it is available in a regional centre costs the hours during which the duct completes its closure. The infusion is both treatment and a diagnostic trial. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital heart disease in the newborn)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital heart disease in the newborn

explanation.summary: Duct dependent systemic circulation, most often critical coarctation or interrupted aortic arch, presents as circulatory collapse in the first two weeks as the arterial duct closes. The physical signature is absent or weak femoral pulses with easily palpable brachial pulses and a pre ductal to post ductal saturation difference, often without any murmur. A normal newborn examination does not exclude it because the duct is still open at discharge. Prostaglandin E1 reopens the duct and is started on clinical grounds, before echocardiography, in any collapsed neonate in whom the diagnosis is possible.
key_points: Absent femoral pulses with present brachial pulses is the key discriminator from sepsis
A pre ductal and post ductal saturation difference greater than 3 percent supports a duct dependent lesion
Absence of a murmur does not exclude critical left heart obstruction
Apnoea is a recognised adverse effect of prostaglandin infusion, so airway support must be immediately available
explanation.pearls: Give prostaglandin E1 and take blood cultures and antibiotics at the same time: the two diagnoses are clinically indistinguishable at the bedside, and treating only for sepsis in a duct dependent lesion is fatal within hours.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Congenital heart disease in the newborn

subtopic_detail: Persistent fever thirty six hours after a first immunoglobulin infusion in Kawasaki disease
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar looking after a 3 year old girl admitted four days ago. She had eight days of fever with bilateral non purulent conjunctival injection, cracked red lips, a polymorphous truncal rash and swollen hands, and was treated with intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg and aspirin.

Her fever settled for about twelve hours and has now returned, with three readings above 38.5 degrees Celsius in the last 36 hours since the infusion finished. She remains irritable. Blood cultures taken before the infusion are sterile at 48 hours, urine culture is negative, and a repeat chest radiograph is clear. The echocardiogram performed yesterday showed a left anterior descending coronary artery z score of 2.8.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 158 beats per minute, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Irritable, peeling skin at the fingertips, lips still cracked, no new rash, no meningism
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 118 mg/L (less than 5) rising from 96 mg/L, albumin 26 g/L (35-50), platelets 620 x10^9/L, blood and urine cultures sterile at 48 hours
data_table.Treatment given: Intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg completed 36 hours ago, aspirin continuing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add broad spectrum antibiotics and repeat the cultures
options.rationale: Sterile cultures at 48 hours with a clear chest radiograph and negative urine make bacterial infection unlikely, and the mucocutaneous features and rising inflammatory markers fit ongoing vasculitis. Reflexively adding antibiotics here delays the treatment that protects the coronary arteries. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Increase the aspirin dose and continue current observation
options.rationale: Aspirin modifies platelet aggregation and provides symptomatic relief but has no effect on the vasculitic process driving aneurysm formation, and observation alone through resistant disease is what allows dilatation to progress. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Give a second dose of intravenous immunoglobulin
options.rationale: Fever persisting or recurring more than 36 hours after completion of the first infusion defines immunoglobulin resistance, which affects around 10 to 20 percent of children and carries a substantially higher risk of coronary aneurysm. A second infusion of 2 g/kg is the standard first response, and the rising C reactive protein with falling albumin confirms continuing inflammation rather than a resolving illness. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Start infliximab in place of further immunoglobulin
options.rationale: Tumour necrosis factor blockade is an accepted option for disease that resists a second infusion, and some centres use it earlier, but it is not the standard first response to a single episode of resistance in Australian practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Repeat the echocardiogram before changing any treatment
options.rationale: Serial echocardiography is part of surveillance and will be repeated, but a scan result does not alter the decision to re treat resistant disease, and waiting for it wastes time during which inflammation continues. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: Immunoglobulin resistant Kawasaki disease is defined by fever that persists or recurs more than 36 hours after the first infusion finishes, and it occurs in roughly 10 to 20 percent of children. It matters because resistance is the strongest predictor of coronary artery aneurysm. The decision to re treat rests on the fever pattern together with inflammatory markers that are rising rather than falling, not on the echocardiogram. Standard management in Australia is a second infusion of 2 g/kg, with corticosteroid or infliximab reserved for children who fail that.
key_points: The 36 hour mark after completion of the infusion defines resistance
A rising C reactive protein with a falling albumin supports continuing vasculitis rather than intercurrent infection
A coronary z score above 2.5 already indicates dilatation and raises the stakes of under treatment
Aspirin does not treat the vasculitis and its dose is not the lever here
explanation.pearls: Do not wait for repeat imaging to decide on re treatment: a coronary z score can be normal on day 5 and aneurysmal by day 14, so the fever and the inflammatory trend, not the echocardiogram, drive the second dose.
